what_it_does: As transistors shrink below 3 nanometers, chip designers stack two transistors on top of each other — a structure called a CFET (Complementary FET). Connecting wires to both the top and bottom of this stack is attractive because it frees up routing space on the back of the chip, but the standard CFET design requires extra 'tap cells' (dedicated regions that handle electrical grounding) that eat into that routing benefit. This paper introduces the FFET (Flip-FET), which physically flips the lower transistor so that its electrical contacts face outward in both directions — toward the front and back of the chip — eliminating the need for those tap cells. The authors then use a co-optimization approach (jointly tuning the chip's physical design rules and the manufacturing process) to show that synthesized circuit libraries using FFET cells achieve better wiring efficiency than standard approaches.
